To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the plasma concentration of iodoproteins in normal calves exhibits circadian rhythms, and that the time of the acrophases of these rhythms is dependent upon the sequence of light and dark periods in the environment.

the concentration of thyroxin in the plasma of calves shows a 24-h rhythm which is controlled by light and darkness and that the amplitude of the rhythm is not influenced by the mean concentration of the thyroid hormone.

in the normal calf the thyroid gland secretes iodoproteins in an endogenous, circadian rhythm which is controlled by a circadian oscillator in the brain and is synchronized with the external environment by the light-dark cycle.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of circadian rhythms in normal and pathological conditions, with the development of new techniques for their study, and with the application of these techniques to the study of the physiology of the thyroid gland.
the circadian rhythms in the plasma levels of iodoproteins, particularly thyroxine and triiodothyronine.
the circadian rhythms of iodoproteins in the plasma of calves.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the thyroid gland of the normal calf, like that of man, has an inherent capacity for producing a rhythm of secretion of thyroxine which is modified by the environment.
the thyroid gland is not under any form of control by a circadian rhythm.
the thyroid hormone concentration in the blood of calves shows circadian rhythmicity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, under normal circumstances, there is a circadian rhythm of iodoprotein concentration in the blood of normal calves, and this rhythm is influenced by environmental lighting patterns.

the thyroid of the calf is capable of producing a rhythm of secretion of thyroxine which is synchronized with the environment, but the amplitude of the rhythm is small and the mean concentration of circulating thyroxine remains relatively constant.
the concentration of thyroxin in the plasma of the calf shows a rhythm of approximately 24 h duration which is controlled by the environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a circadian rhythm of thyroid hormone levels in the plasma of calves.

we can’t rely on our circadian clocks alone to keep us on a healthy sleep schedule, but that we can use our knowledge of our circadian rhythms and how they are affected by external factors to help us get better sleep and improve our health.
